== Response

Actions::
* Kind: containment; What: Enable the rate limit and block the abusive address ranges; Role: role:developer; Issues: ID-901; Done: yes
* Kind: recovery; What: Force a password reset for the accounts that were reached from the blocked ranges; Role: role:service-owner; Issues: ID-902; Done: yes

Timeline::
* At: 2026-11-10T13:15:00Z; What: The alert on failed logins fires.
* At: 2026-11-10T15:20:00Z; What: The abusive address ranges are blocked.
* At: 2026-11-12T09:00:00Z; What: No further attempts from the blocked ranges for a day; the incident is closed.

Resolved at:: 2026-11-12T09:00:00Z

== Review

Root causes::
* Category: configuration; Description: The rate limit of the login form counted per session, so a client without cookies was never limited.
* Category: access-control; Description: Passwords from public leaks were still accepted when a user chose them.

Measures::
* What: Limit the attempts per address range and per account; Role: role:developer; Issues: ID-911; Due: 2026-12-15
* What: Check new passwords against a list of leaked ones; Role: role:developer; Issues: ID-912; Due: 2027-01-31

== Course

The alert on failed logins fired within minutes. The traffic came from a few address ranges and tried leaked credentials at a high rate. Blocking the ranges and enabling the rate limit stopped it within two hours.

== Root-cause analysis

The login form limited the attempts per session only, so a client that sent no cookie was never limited. In addition, passwords that are known from public leaks were still accepted at sign-up and at a password change.

== Lessons

The alert and the block list worked as intended; two gaps remain.

* The limit must apply per address range and per account.
* New passwords must be checked against known leaks.
